system:
You are the Issuing authority reviewer, standing in for the national emergency authority that issues alerts (who, where, when). You check that this sender may issue this alert, for this area, now: the sender is in the issuer register, the target area is the one requested for this event, the status fits the context (a drill stays a drill), it does not overreach an active alert from a higher authority, and a correction points to the alert it corrects.
You see only the issuer register, active and earlier alerts, the requested area and the alert's status, type, sender and area. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

The recording that the midnight shift supervisor plays over the phone contains the text of an EAS message for a live ballistic missile alert, including the language, “this is not a drill,” instead of the language used in HIEMA’s standard operating procedure for this drill. Although the midnight shift officer’s recorded voice reads, “Exercise, Exercise, Exercise” at the beginning and end of the drill, using the phrase “this is not a drill” was a deviation from the drill procedure. When the alert origination software prompts the warning officer to confirm whether the officer wants to send the message, the prompt reads, “Are you sure that you want to send this Alert?” The prompt contains the same message, irrespective of whether the message is a test or an alert, and it does not offer the officer an opportunity to review the message text that would be sent. [FCC-HI-2018#0084] Report and Recommendations: Hawaii Emergency Management Agency January 13, 2018 False Alert (p.15): HI-EMA’s procedures for conducting a ballistic missile drill lacked adequate safeguards that might have helped to avoid the communication errors that led to the false alert.74 First, the ballistic missile checklist lacked guidelines for HI-EMA staff for conducting an internal drill, including how to create or modify an internal drill initiation message.75 As a matter of general practice, the HI-EMA procedure for an internal drill used language identical to that contained in the checklist for actual ballistic missile alerts—including the phrase “real world”—but added the words “exercise, exercise, exercise” both before and after the message to indicate that it was a drill. Use of the same language for both test and live alert initiation procedures could cause confusion among warning officers who received the message without prior notice, notwithstanding the statements at the beginning and end of the message that it was an exercise. HI-EMA’s alert origination software vendor intends to clearly differentiate its test environment from its live alert environment (e.g., color coding and alphabetizing their templates, and adding information to its final confirmation prompt (speedbump) that makes clear whether the alert about to be sent is a live alert). data.summary: The sender is in the issuer register (level 1, all areas and categories). The area matches the area drawn for uae-dust-drill. There are no active alerts from higher authorities to overreach, and no correction reference is needed for msgType Alert. Status Exercise fits the drill context. However, this exercise is set to scope Public and is being sent from a live console environment, so it could reach the public's devices. Whether a public-facing drill on the live system is intended is a decision for a person.

objections.issue: An exercise-status alert with scope Public is being prepared in the live console environment, so it could be broadcast to the public. Drill guidance says drill messages should stay off consumer devices and that test and live environments should be clearly separated. A person must confirm that public distribution of this drill is intended and authorised; otherwise it should be restricted or moved to a test environment.
objections.fix: A responsible person should confirm that a public drill broadcast on the live system is intended. If it is not, change scope to Restricted or Private, or send the alert from a test environment.
